title: Retro Over-the-air Weather Channel
blurb: Real time weather over RF airwaves to vintage TVs.
overview: An Open House event at the local Nova Labs makerspace needed exhibits and demos. I had previously been experimenting with local RF signal broadcasting and put together a custom Nova Labs weather channel using the Weatherstar 4000+ open source project.

diary.title: Day 1 — RF Testing
diary.body: Picked up and tested an RF transmitter. Local station channel 11 with NTSC video signal and audio was eventually chosen and configured.

diary.title: Day 2 — Broadcast Sample
diary.body: A laptop and a Playdate handheld game console used the Playdate's Mirror application to view the FMV Game Blippo+ via the RF transmitter to a black and white TV.

diary.title: Day 3 — Raspberry Pi Portable Board
diary.body: A raspberry pi and the RF transmitter and a power strip were mounted to a pegboard so the broadcast system could be easily moved for exhibit displays.

diary.title: Day 4 - Open House
diary.body: The open source project Weatherstar 4000+ was hosted on github pages and the raspberry pi acts as a kiosk to view it. A display at Nova Labs makerspace open house was prepared to broadcast it to multiple vintage TVs over the air.

title: Pizza Time
blurb: Foam and fabric portable pizza oven.
overview: A Halloween event prompted to decorate a vehicle for trick-or-treaters. I decided on a pizza restaurant theme, and needed the back of my vehicle to appear to contain a brick pizza oven. Foam insulation board was used for the faux brick, and the oven flame effect was produced with a laser projector on a bedsheet and a number of portable fans to animate the projection surface. I prepared costumes and props, which allowed for a server and two kitchen chefs to seat and serve children their Halloween candy as though they were at an outdoor restaurant.

diary.title: Concept
diary.body: A rough sketch for the concept. Ensuring the oven opening sizing properly matched a real pizza peel prop which would be used to serve candy to trick-or-treaters. The oven chimney atop the car and pizza themed wheel cover ideas would be cut due to time and complexity constraints.

diary.title: Texture tests
diary.body: Turning foam into brick would need to be convincing. Insulation foam board will deform when a heat gun is applied, and it will have interesting organic patterns when sprayed with water before heat treatment. This approach was interesting, but eventually abandoned, and other avenues would be explored.

diary.title: Paint testing
diary.body: Brick used in building construction and brick used in ovens have distinct differences. Construction brick is often blemished with white-ish mortar or the remnants of removed siding or other adhered materials. Some red brick may be uniform, but layered reds and browns applied with a sponge give an illusion of depth, with shadow and highlights.

diary.title: Brick carving
diary.body: The oven opening, using the size determined previously, and the brick pattern was sharpie'd on. A heated soldering iron was used to carve the brick by melting the foam insulation board which appears organic and non-uniform. A stiff wire brush was used to texture the insulation board for a convincing brick-like appearance.

diary.title: Archway assembly
diary.body: Some insulation board from the removed oven opening was used to cut and shape individual bricks, which would border the opening for additional depth.

diary.title: Painting and portability
diary.body: The brick surface and concrete base were painted using colors from paint testing. A blackened creosete/smoke appearance was added above the oven's opening. The oven was then bisected so it could be transported in the vehicle with passengers and installed within it. This was necessary as the geometry of the rear opening of the vehicle was smaller than the interior cargo area within.

diary.title: Oven flame projector testing
diary.body: The oven would look most impressive in the dark if its interior was animated with glowing flame. This obviously can't be done practically without being dangerous. This video demonstrates how a battery-powered projector with a red light pattern, a bedsheet, and some portable fans were used to simulate the hearth's toasty insides.

diary.title: Day-of setup
diary.body: The installation and props for the pizza kitchen, with various implements for serving candy to trick-or-treaters.

diary.title: Showtime
diary.body: Actors were costumed for interacting with trick-or-treaters, and gave candy and fake moustaches. A wet towel was used to simulate a pizza dough and an actor tossed it about while interacting to animate the scene. Another actor seated the children at the table and took their dinner orders for, what else, but candy.

title: EKG Machine Clue Cabinet
blurb: Animated, aged, abandoned hospital equipment with a secret.
overview: A local escape room was seeking collaboration with local propmakers. After some consultation, I was asked to create a new and engaging container for an existing puzzle clue. The theme for the escape room was a midcentury abandoned hospital. We decided on a piece of abandoned medical machinery. It would incorporate a distressed appearance, a keypad, a magnetic locking, spring-loaded hidden door, an animated display, and some engaging dials, buttons, and knobs.

diary.title: The Escape Room
diary.body: This abandoned wartime hospital room was in need of a unique piece for clue storage behind a keypad lock. The client requested that it accommodate an existing object's dimensions inside, fit beneath the existing wall guard, and accommodate concealed electrical connection to the outlet. It would be bracketed permanently to the wall with a zero-clearance gap, so escape game players would not reach behind it. It would contain a hidden drawer to contain the clue, which should be non-removable to prevent curious gamers from damaging it.

diary.title: Design
diary.body: Initial concept sketches.

diary.title: References
diary.body: 1940s EKG machines were initially paper-fed and needle-marked like a seismograph. Others later used an oscilloscope display which would be both more interesting looking and also more cost effective and reliable to recreate without requiring frequent service. Wooden furniture like a potato storage box had an angled upper portion which could be interesting for a control panel, but a piece of medical equipment like an oscilloscope wasn't the same as a control console. The initial angled display console concept changed to something more like the pictured soviet lab equipment, mixed with the authentic ribbon and paper machine. Highly weathered rust effects would be desired and reference textures were recorded.

diary.title: CNC Parts
diary.body: The ShopSabre CNC router machine would be used to create precision cuts for multiple materials and overlays for the face of the device. The acrylic lens, the bezels of the front panel, and the voids on the front and the back would be routed in with this process.

diary.title: Display Animation, Panel Elements
diary.body: A panel would display the oscilloscope style animation. Multiple animation tests and concepts were used on a 64x64 display originally used in a child's novelty backpack, repurposed for its unusual mix of large size and low resolution. Additional switch and dial greebling was achived by including an unusual piece of vintage photography darkroom equipment. It contained very unfamiliar looking dials, markings, and meters and atmospheric lighting that looked great in darker areas.

diary.title: Hidden Drawer
diary.body: The interior dimensions of the drawer were the most imporant part of the build, due to the size of the pre-existing object that needed to be stored inside. It dictated many of the prop's final dimensions. A period appropriate, maintenance-free, highly durable slideless drawer design was implemented. It needed to have no vertical or horizontal play, as well as inability to be fully removed or extended to prevent tampering by escape gamers. The magnetic lock's connection plate needed to remain inaccessible and have a mountable surface for adjustable positioning of the spring-loaded addition.

diary.title: Weathering and final assembly
diary.body: The prop was given a rust and water-damaged appearance. Spraypaint over beaded water was able to provide realistic rust paint bubbling on display elements. Wood stain and stain correction markers of incorrect colors were used to simulate water damage stains.

diary.title: Completed prop
diary.body: The keypad was wired to the magnetic lock, and all components were powered.

title: In Progress: Banana For Scale
blurb: An exploration of scale and low-cost material.
overview: I've always been delighted by small versions of big things or big versions of small things. I was interested in creating a larger-than-convenient build of something mundane at extremely low cost. After a bit of research, cardboard seemed like the perfect route to make my dreams come true. A banana is a universally renowned measurement of scale, so why not complicate things? This is currently an uncomissioned work in progress.

diary.title: References
diary.body: Bananas in various ripening stages. Eventually one would be taken to a local home center for paint color matching.

diary.title: Quick Test #1
diary.body: A single peel slice was produced in cardboard and acrylic paints from memory for color, size, and shape. Sticker was borrowed from lunch.

diary.title: 3D Print
diary.body: A durable, perpetual, realistic 3D print banana was produced. The color matched paint from the real banana was used to surprising success.

diary.title: 3D Cardboard + Waterproof Coating Test
diary.body: A cosplay technique of wrapping a body part in cling film and then duct tape, and drawing the contours of an object onto the tape could be applied to the banana to produce a papercraft model. The tape was removed, cut, and affixed to cardboard to transfer the pattern. The shape was cut with a number of tabs which would allow it to be glued to its neighboring pieces. An experimental waterproof coating of melted beeswax and shellac was prepared and applied to the surface of the cardboard and allowed to dry before painting. Unfortunately the beeswax did not emulsify in the alcohol when cooling so it gives the banana a very bumpy appearance, and the acrylic paint and shellac give it a very glossy, un-banana finish. Detail testing was lazily applied for brown ripening coloring. Another approach would be necessary.

diary.title: Cardboard slices test
diary.body: With a little math help from an AI chatbot, 170 roughly 10x10 inch cardboard panels were cut from whole boxes and stacked in order for relatively similar dimensions. The resulting stack was under 3 feet tall, but appeared to be rather heavy and very dense. This could not be carved as is. Another approach would be necessary.

diary.title: Cardboard slices stacking test.
diary.body: Cutting a 3 foot loose cardboard sculpture is not easily achievable, so we attempted to approach doing it in sections. A jigsaw blade's length was used to determine the maximum size of a stack that could be cut with that tool safely. Panels were glued together with wood glue and clamped overnight. The resulting panel was very rigid and very strong, like very lightweight wood. The jigsaw did not fair easily and multiple blades were consumed in just this minor attempt at tapering the tip. Most jigsaw cuts are on 3/4 inch material or thinner. Not material the entire length of the blade. Thinner slices could be assembled, but carving consistency between thin layers would present a challenge. Another approach would be necessary.

diary.title: Foam test
diary.body: A product at the local home center advertised creating an expanding foam to fill a deck post hole and replaced 2 50LB bags of concrete. We expected this would generate a significant volume of foam that could be carved. The largest box available was coated with silicone lubricant to act as a mold release and the two-part foam reagents were mixed and poured inside. We had not accounted for the interior flaps of the box, and the foam reagents settled beneath two panels which prevented them from expanding fully. The central area was not suficient for carving, and a can of expanding foam was tested to determine it's maximum volume to attempt to save the experimentation. It was much less dense and did not yield consistent material or enough volume to provide a carving substrate. Another approach would be necessary.

diary.title: 3D Puzzle Cardboard Test
diary.body: A 3D Model used for the 3D printed banana was manipulated to generate a sliced series of interlocking vector shapes, which, when printed, cut, and assembled, act as a 3D puzzle to produce the end shape in a skeleton-like model. A laser cutter was leveraged to cut the interlocking slices at the largest size the laser could accommodate. This yielded a 35 inch long banana when assembled, over 38 inches with the curve if it were straight. This is the first successful large banana progress in many days. If damaged in further testing, it can be reproduced in under 1 hour for about $6 from two new large size cardboard boxes.

diary.title: 3D Puzzle Skin Trial
diary.body: The outer skin would be made of brown recycled kraft paper. A rough panel was measured and cut and affixed with glue. The result makes the skeleton ribs of the 3D model very prominent. Initially a minimum number of paper sheets were going to be used to simulate the continuous appearance of an unbroken banana peel which lacks many textures that would result from a paper mache type covering. Once completed, another filler material will need to be applied and shaped to give an even surface.

diary.title: To be continued!
diary.body: Not everything we try to make gets made the way we wanted. Make-fail is part of the process whenever trying something new. Check here for further updates as this project continues.

title: Hammer of Thor
overview: I came across an incredible model of Thor's hammer which I couldn't wait to 3D print. Printed in matte black, within a few hours I used dry brushing technique to bring this to life. Additional touches of leather and jute gave even more textures to this hero prop. Model credits to Oliver as @Darkwiese on Makerworld. Uncommissioned.

diary.title: Model
diary.body: This model was printed overnight and utilized the maximum dimensions of the Bambu X1 Carbon. Quick turnaround and low cost.

diary.title: Paint and dress
diary.body: In under 24 hours, I produced this 1:1 scale set-ready hero prop from materials to finished.
